tips.title: Unlimited liability means personal possessions
tips.body: A **sole trader** and an ordinary **partnership** have **unlimited** liability: the owner's own house and savings are at risk. A private limited company has **limited** liability, so only what was invested is at risk.

tips.title: Franchisor owns, franchisee buys
tips.body: The **franchisor** owns the brand and sells the right to use it. The **franchisee** pays to run one outlet. The word ending in *-ee* is the one paying, as with employee and employer.

tips.title: All four Ps have to agree
tips.body: A premium price with cheap packaging and discount-shop distribution does not work. Whenever you change one part of the marketing mix, say what it means for the others: that consistency is where the marks are.

tips.title: Check each P against the customer
tips.body: The four Ps only earn marks when they **fit the target market**. Take each in turn and finish the sentence *…because the customer is…*. A price, a place or a promotion with no customer attached is a description, and description sits in the bottom band.

steps.title: One owner: the sole trader
steps.body:
A **sole trader** is a business owned by one person. It is the simplest structure and the most common: plumbers, hairdressers, market stalls, freelance designers.

The owner makes every decision, keeps all the profit, and can set up almost immediately with very little paperwork.

The cost is **unlimited liability**. In law the owner and the business are the same thing, so if the business cannot pay its debts, the owner's personal possessions, their car, savings and even their home, can be taken to pay them. The other drawbacks follow from being alone: long hours, no one to cover illness or holidays, and finance limited to what one person can borrow.

visuals.problem: Meet Priya, who bakes cakes from her kitchen

steps.text: Priya sets up as a sole trader: no forms beyond telling the tax office, and she starts trading that week
She keeps every pound of profit and decides everything: prices, hours, what to bake
A big wedding order is cancelled after she has bought the ingredients on credit. She cannot pay the supplier
Unlimited liability: the supplier can pursue Priya personally, not just the business

steps.title: Partners and private limited companies
steps.body:
A **partnership** is owned by two or more people. Partners share the capital, the work, the skills and the decisions, so there is cover for holidays and more money to start with. They also share the profit, they can disagree, and in an ordinary partnership every partner still has **unlimited liability**, for the whole debt, including debts another partner ran up.

A **private limited company** (Ltd) is different in kind. It is **incorporated**: registered at Companies House as a separate legal person from its owners. The owners are **shareholders**, and their liability is **limited** to what they paid for their shares. The company can raise money by selling more shares, though only privately, not to the public.

The price is paperwork and openness: accounts must be filed and can be read by anyone, and there is more law to follow.

steps.title: Buying into a brand: franchising
steps.body:
A **franchise** is not a legal structure like the three above; it is a way of starting. The **franchisor** owns a brand, a product and a proven way of running the business. The **franchisee** pays for the right to use them: an initial fee, then an ongoing **royalty**, usually a percentage of revenue.

What the franchisee gets: a name customers already trust, training, national advertising, bulk-bought supplies, and a model that is known to work, so far fewer franchises fail than independent start-ups.

What the franchisee gives up: independence. The franchisor decides the products, the prices, the shop fit and the rules, and a slice of every sale leaves the business for ever.

A franchisee can still be a sole trader, a partnership or a limited company; the franchise sits on top of whichever they choose.

steps.title: Where to put the business
steps.body:
Location can decide whether a business survives, and the right answer depends on what the business does. The factors to weigh:

- **Proximity to the market**: how close to customers. Essential for a café, a hairdresser, a repair shop, anything the customer has to visit.
- **Proximity to labour**: whether people with the right skills live nearby, and what they cost.
- **Proximity to materials**: for businesses that use heavy or bulky inputs, being near the supply cuts transport costs.
- **Proximity to competitors**: sometimes to avoid them, sometimes to join them, because a street of restaurants draws more diners than one alone.

Against all of these sits **cost**. A town centre has footfall and high rent; an industrial estate has cheap space and no passers-by. The nature of the business decides which matters more.

steps.title: How the internet changed the map
steps.body:
**E-commerce**, selling online, has rewritten the location decision for many small businesses.

If customers buy on a website, they never visit, so the business does not need a shop where people walk past. It can run from a cheap unit, or a spare room, and still sell to the whole country. Fixed costs fall, the market grows, and a business can open with far less money.

The internet does not remove location altogether. The business still needs somewhere to work, to keep stock, and to send parcels from, so being near good transport links and cheap space now matters more than being near customers.

And some businesses cannot move online. You cannot cut hair or repair a bike over a website, so those still need to be where their customers are.

Lena sells from a website, working from a garage: no rent, customers anywhere in the UK

Sam's shop gives customers the smell and the look, which a website cannot

steps.title: The marketing mix: four Ps that must agree
steps.body:
The **marketing mix** is the set of decisions a business makes to sell to its target market. There are four, and they all begin with P:

- **Product**: what is sold, including its design, quality, features and brand.
- **Price**: what customers pay, and what that price says about the product.
- **Promotion**: how customers find out about it: advertising, social media, special offers.
- **Place**: where and how it is sold: a shop, a website, through other retailers.

The point that earns marks is that the four **must work together**. A luxury handbag with a high price, sold in a discount supermarket and promoted with buy-one-get-one-free offers, sends four different messages, and customers trust none of them. Every element has to fit the same target customer.

check.prompt: A business sells a premium, high-priced skincare range. Which promotion would be inconsistent with the rest of its marketing mix?
check.solution: Permanent discounts in a bargain shop tell customers the product is cheap, which contradicts the premium price and undermines the brand. The other three fit a high-end product.

steps.title: When the customer changes, the mix changes
steps.body:
The mix is not set once. Two things keep forcing it to move.

**Changing consumer needs.** Customers now want convenience, ethical sourcing, healthier options, personalisation. A business that keeps selling what its customers used to want loses them to one that noticed.

**Technology.** E-commerce changes *place*. Social media and digital advertising change *promotion*, and make it cheap enough for the smallest business. Online comparison puts pressure on *price*, and lets some businesses change prices by the hour. Reviews and data even change the *product*, because businesses can see what customers actually use.

In an exam, take each change in the case study and ask which P it hits and what the business should do about it.

steps.title: The business plan
steps.body:
A **business plan** is a written document that sets out what the business will do and how. Start-ups write one for three reasons:

1. **To set aims and objectives**, so the owner knows what success looks like and can measure progress against it.
2. **To reduce risk**. Forecasting revenue, costs and cash flow on paper finds problems, such as running out of cash in month three, before real money is lost.
3. **To secure finance**. A bank or investor will not lend to a business that cannot show its forecasts and its market.

What goes in it: the business idea, the aims and objectives, the target market and the competition, the forecast revenue, costs and profit, a cash-flow forecast, the sources of finance, the location, and the marketing mix.

One honest limit: a plan is built from forecasts, and forecasts can be wrong. It reduces risk; it does not remove it.

steps.title: Your turn: read the case, pick the structure
steps.body:
Here is a case in the style of Paper 1, Section B. Read it, then answer the check. The skill is matching what the case *says* to the structure that fits: how many owners, how much money is at risk, where the finance will come from.

**Case:** Tom and Aisha have been making furniture in a rented workshop for a year. They want to lease a bigger unit and buy machinery costing £80 000. They have £15 000 between them. Aisha's parents have offered to invest £30 000 if they get a share of the business, and a bank has offered a loan for the rest.

steps.title: Going deeper: how the 9 and 12 markers are marked
steps.body:
The theory in this topic is not hard. The grades separate on the long questions, and they are marked on **how you argue**, not how much you know.

**Analyse (6 marks).** Two chains of reasoning. Each starts from a fact in the case, moves through *this means... which leads to...*, and ends in an effect on sales, costs, profit or reputation. Two short chains beat one long list.

**Justify (9 marks).** Choose. Argue for your choice *and* against the other, both applied to the case. Then a judgement that names the deciding factor: *because the business has little finance*, *because customers must visit*, *because £80 000 is at risk*.

**Evaluate (12 marks).** Both sides, developed and applied. Then the sentence examiners are waiting for: *it depends on...* Name what it depends on, and say how the answer would change if that thing were different.

Every paragraph must contain a word from the case study. An answer that would be true of any business scores at the bottom level.

check.solution: Level 3 needs a conclusion that is valid and well reasoned, which means saying what it depends on and how the answer would change. Both sides, application and a judgement are all required, but without the *it depends on* the answer stays at level 3.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Sole trader**: one owner, all the profit, all the decisions, **unlimited liability**.
- **Partnership**: two or more owners, shared capital and skills, shared profit, still **unlimited liability**.
- **Private limited company**: incorporated, owned by shareholders, **limited liability**, can sell shares privately, must file accounts.
- **Franchise**: pay a fee and royalties to use a proven brand and model; less risk, less independence, less profit kept.
- **Location** depends on the business: near customers for services people visit, near materials for heavy inputs, cheap space for businesses customers never see.
- **E-commerce** lets a business sell nationally from a low-cost location, but services that need the customer present still have to be near them.
- **Marketing mix**: product, price, promotion, place, and they must **agree with each other** and with the target market.
- **Changing needs and technology** move the mix: ask which P each change hits.
- **Business plan**: sets objectives, reduces risk, secures finance. Built on forecasts, so it reduces risk rather than removing it.
- **Long answers**: chains from the case, argue both ways, judge, and say what it depends on.

questions.prompt: Ravi runs a small independent clothing shop in a market town. Sales have fallen since a large online retailer started offering next-day delivery in the area. Analyse the impact of technology on the marketing mix of Ravi's business.
questions.solution: Two developed chains, each applied to Ravi. Place: customers now buy online, so Ravi's shop loses sales to next-day delivery; if he adds his own online shop he can reach customers beyond the town, which recovers some sales. Promotion: social media lets him show new stock to local customers cheaply, which brings them into the shop, at a fraction of the cost of print advertising. Level 3 needs both chains to end in an effect on sales, costs or profit.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Place: online buying has changed where Ravi's customers shop, applied to the fall in sales
Developed to an outcome: an online shop of his own could reach customers outside the town and recover sales
Promotion or price: social media promotion, or the pressure on price from online comparison, applied to Ravi
Developed to an outcome: lower promotion costs and more local footfall, or a decision on price

questions.modelAnswer: Technology has changed the *place* element of Ravi's mix. His customers can now buy clothes online with next-day delivery, so they no longer need to visit his shop, which is why sales have fallen. If Ravi set up his own online store, he could sell to customers beyond the market town, so the fall in shop sales might be offset by online sales, protecting his revenue. Technology also changes *promotion*. Ravi could use social media to show new stock to local customers for almost no cost, which would bring more of them into the shop and reduce his spending on print advertising, so his promotion costs fall while footfall rises. Both effects mean Ravi has to change his mix rather than keep the one that worked before the online retailer arrived.

questions.prompt: Jess has run a successful mobile dog-grooming business as a sole trader for three years. She wants to open a salon and take on a second groomer. Analyse the benefits to Jess of changing the business to a partnership.
questions.solution: Two chains, both about Jess. Finance: a partner brings capital, so the salon fit-out can be paid for without a large loan, so less interest is paid. Skills and cover: a partner shares the work and the decisions, so Jess can take time off without losing bookings, and a second groomer's skills widen what the salon offers. A grade 9 answer notes the partnership still has unlimited liability, so it does not solve every problem.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Benefit: a partner brings capital, applied to the cost of opening a salon
Developed to an outcome: less borrowing, so less interest, or the salon opens sooner
Benefit: shared workload, skills or decisions, applied to a mobile business becoming a salon

questions.modelAnswer: A partner would bring capital into the business. Opening a salon means paying for premises and equipment, so a partner's investment would reduce how much Jess has to borrow, which means lower interest payments and less risk if the salon is slow to fill. A partner also shares the work and the decisions. At the moment Jess cannot take a holiday without cancelling bookings; with a partner the salon can stay open, so customers are kept, and a second groomer's skills let the salon offer services Jess cannot, which increases revenue. The partnership still has unlimited liability, but for a business of this size the extra capital and cover are the benefits that matter.

questions.prompt: Two friends plan to open a bakery. They have savings of £20 000 between them and need £60 000 in total. One wants to set up as a partnership; the other wants a private limited company. Justify which structure they should choose.
questions.solution: Choose, argue for it and against the other, then a judgement naming the deciding factor. The stronger case is the private limited company: they need £40 000 more than they have, a company can raise it by selling shares to family or investors, and limited liability protects their savings if the bakery fails, which matters when £60 000 is at stake. Against the partnership: unlimited liability and no shares to sell. The judgement: it depends on how they will raise the £40 000; if a bank loan is the plan, the extra paperwork of a company matters less than the protection it gives.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear choice is made and reasons given for it, applied to the £40 000 shortfall or the risk
Reasons given against the other structure, applied to the case
A judgement that names the deciding factor, such as the size of the debt or where the finance will come from

questions.modelAnswer: They should form a private limited company. They need £40 000 more than their savings, and a company can raise money by selling shares to family or investors, which a partnership cannot do. A company also gives the two friends limited liability: if the bakery fails, they lose only what they invested, and their homes are safe, which matters when £60 000 is being put into a bakery that might not succeed. A partnership is quicker to set up and has less paperwork, but it leaves both friends with unlimited liability for the whole debt, and they would have to borrow all of the shortfall. The deciding factor is the amount of money at risk. With £60 000 invested in a new bakery that might not succeed, the protection of limited liability outweighs the extra administration, so the private limited company is the better choice.

questions.prompt: Amara makes handmade jewellery. She is deciding between renting a small unit in a busy shopping centre and selling only through her own website from home. Justify which location she should choose.
questions.solution: Either choice can score full marks if justified. Website: no rent, so lower fixed costs and lower risk; customers across the country, not one town; jewellery is light and cheap to post. Against the shopping centre: high rent must be paid before a single sale, and a small unit reaches only local shoppers. The judgement should name what it depends on: her finance and whether her customers need to see the jewellery in person.

questions.modelAnswer: Amara should sell through her website. Jewellery is light and easy to post, so she can reach customers all over the country instead of only the people who walk past one shop, which gives her a far larger market. Working from home means no rent, so her fixed costs are low and she does not have to make sales just to cover the unit each month, which reduces the risk of the business failing early. A shopping centre unit would give her passing trade and let customers see and try the jewellery, which can matter for a product people like to touch, but the rent has to be paid whether or not anyone buys, and a start-up making handmade items may not sell enough to cover it. The deciding factor is fixed cost against reach: because her product travels well and her finances are small, the website gives her more customers at less risk, so it is the better choice now, with a shop something to consider once sales are established.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether writing a detailed business plan guarantees that a new business will succeed.
questions.solution: Both sides, then a judgement with it depends on. For: a plan forces the owner to research the market and forecast cash flow, so problems are found before money is spent, and it secures finance. Against: forecasts are estimates and can be wrong; external factors such as a new competitor or a recession are not in the owner's control; a plan does not make the owner good at running the business. Judgement: a plan reduces risk but cannot guarantee success; how much it helps depends on how realistic the forecasts are and on what happens in the market after opening.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 4): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge, applied at least a little, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to this business, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion
Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains and a well-reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer: A detailed business plan makes success more likely, but it cannot guarantee it. Writing the plan forces the owner to research the target market and forecast revenue, costs and cash flow, which means problems such as running out of cash in the first months are found on paper before any money is spent, so the owner can change the idea or raise more finance in time. The plan also matters for finance: a bank will not lend without one, so a good plan can be the difference between opening and not opening. On the other hand, every number in the plan is a forecast, and forecasts can be wrong; if the market turns out to be smaller than estimated, the plan gives false confidence. External influences are not in the plan's control, so a recession or a new competitor can undo the best forecast, and a plan does not make the owner good at managing staff or customers day to day. Overall, a plan reduces risk rather than removing it. How far it helps depends on how realistic the forecasts were and on what happens in the market after the business opens, so the same plan could lead to success in one year and failure in another.

questions.prompt: A partnership of three accountants has unlimited liability. Which statement about the partners' risk is correct?
questions.solution: In an ordinary partnership every partner is liable for all of the business's debts, including those caused by another partner, and their personal possessions are at risk. That shared exposure is why partners must trust each other, and why some choose a company instead.

markScheme.description: each partner liable for all debts, personal possessions at risk

options: Only the partner who caused a debt is liable for it
Each partner can lose personal possessions to pay a debt, even one run up by another partner
Each partner is only liable for one third of the debt
The partners are only liable for the capital they each invested

questions.prompt: A new bicycle repair business wants to keep its start-up costs as low as possible and must be somewhere customers can bring their bikes. Which location factor should weigh most in its decision?
questions.solution: The nature of the business decides. A repair service cannot be done online and customers have to get there, so being close to them matters more than anything else. Parts are light and can be delivered, so materials do not decide it.

markScheme.description: proximity to the market, because the service needs the customer to visit

options: Proximity to competitors, so it can copy their prices
Proximity to the market, because customers must physically bring their bikes
Proximity to raw materials, because parts are heavy
The internet, because it can repair bikes online

questions.prompt: A small café has noticed that its customers increasingly want plant-based food, want to order on their phones, and want to know where ingredients come from. Analyse how the café should change its marketing mix in response to these changing consumer needs.
questions.skill: changing consumer needs and the mix
questions.solution: Two chains, each starting from one of the three needs. Product: add plant-based dishes and label the source of ingredients, so the café keeps customers who would otherwise go elsewhere, so revenue is protected. Place or promotion: phone ordering means adding an app or an ordering website and promoting the sourcing story on social media, so convenience and trust bring repeat customers. Each chain must end in sales, costs or customer loyalty.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Product change identified from the case: plant-based dishes or ingredient sourcing
Developed to an outcome for the café: customers retained, revenue protected, or a higher price justified
Place or promotion change identified from the case: phone ordering, or promoting provenance
Developed to an outcome: convenience brings repeat business, or trust supports loyalty

questions.modelAnswer: The café should change its *product* first. Customers want plant-based food, so adding several plant-based dishes keeps those customers, who would otherwise go to a competitor, which protects the café's revenue; showing where ingredients come from on the menu gives customers the information they are asking for, which builds trust and may justify a slightly higher price. It should also change *place* and *promotion*. Customers want to order on their phones, so adding an ordering app or website makes buying more convenient, which encourages repeat orders and could add takeaway sales the café did not have before, and promoting the sourcing story on social media reaches the customers who care about it at almost no cost. Together these changes keep the four Ps consistent with what the café's customers now want, rather than what they wanted when it opened.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a feature of a private limited company?
questions.solution: A **private** limited company may not sell shares to the **general public** — that is what separates it from a public limited company. Its owners have **limited** liability.

markScheme.description: shares cannot be sold to the general public

options: It must be owned by one person
Its shares cannot be sold to the general public
Its shares are traded on the stock exchange
Its owners have unlimited liability

questions.prompt: Which of the four Ps is being changed when a business moves its products into supermarkets as well as its own shop?
questions.solution: **Place** is where and how the product reaches the customer. Selling through supermarkets as well as its own shop changes the **place**, not what the product is or what it costs.

markScheme.description: place

options: Price
Product
Promotion
Place

examTechnique.body:
Section 1.4 supplies the short questions in Section A and, more importantly, the context for the long ones in Sections B and C: a case study about a start-up choosing a structure, a location or a mix is the classic Paper 1 material. The definitions must be exact, because the multiple-choice distractors are the near misses: partnership against private limited company, unlimited against limited liability, franchisor against franchisee.

The marks that decide the grade are in the 6, 9 and 12 mark questions, and they are lost the same way every year: generic answers that never mention the business in the case, single points instead of chains, and 9 and 12 markers with no judgement, or a judgement that does not say what it depends on.
examinerErrors: Saying a partnership has limited liability. An ordinary partnership does not; every partner is liable for the whole debt.
Confusing franchisor and franchisee. The franchisor owns the brand and receives the fees; the franchisee pays them and runs the outlet.
Listing all four location factors instead of picking the one the case makes decisive and explaining why.
Describing the four Ps separately without saying that they have to be consistent with each other and with the target market.
Writing that a business plan guarantees success, or makes profit. It reduces risk and helps secure finance; the forecasts inside it can be wrong.
Long answers with no word from the case study in them. An answer that is true of any business is capped at the bottom level, however good the theory.
Ending a 12 marker without it depends on. That sentence, with the condition named, is the difference between level 3 and level 4.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer quotes the case in every paragraph and never argues in general. For a structure question it names the facts that decide it, how many owners, how much is at risk, where the money will come from, and picks the structure those facts point to. For a location or a mix question it identifies which factor or which P the case has changed and follows the chain through to sales, costs or profit. Its 9 markers argue for and against and end by naming the deciding factor; its 12 markers weigh both sides and finish with it depends on, the condition named, and what would change if the condition were different.
